title: Arrays & Hashing
scopeHtml: Scope: complexity estimation, hash-map lookups, frequency counting, prefix sums, Kadane's algorithm. Code is shown in C++, Java, Kotlin and Python tabs.

notes.title: How to use this track and read complexity
notes.html:
Languages. Every code sample in this track is shown in one tabbed window: C++, Java, Kotlin, Python (C++ first because you know it; the others are written the way that language's developers would write them, not translated line by line). Pick a tab and read the same idea in a new language.

How to solve a problem. Interviewers rarely test a trick you must have memorised; they test whether you can recognise a pattern. Use this order every time:

  1. Restate the problem and give 2-3 examples, including an empty and a single-element input.
  2. Brute force first and say its cost out loud (usually O(n²) or worse).
  3. Spot the pattern from the signals listed in each section ("sorted array", "contiguous subarray", "shortest path", "all combinations").
  4. Code the template, then dry-run it on your example.
  5. State complexity (time and extra space) and edge cases.

Complexity cheat sheet. About 10^8 simple operations fit in one second, so the input size tells you the target:

n up to Acceptable Typical pattern
10 to 20 O(2^n), O(n!) backtracking, bitmask
500 O(n³) 3 nested loops, small DP
5,000 O(n²) 2D DP, pairs
10^5 to 10^6 O(n log n), O(n) sort, heap, binary search, two pointers, hashing
10^9 O(log n), O(1) binary search, math

Industry examples. The same patterns are everywhere in production: hash maps in caches and deduplication, sliding windows in rate limiters, heaps in schedulers and top-K dashboards, graphs in maps and dependency resolvers, DP in diff tools and autocorrect.

Everyday analogy. A chess player does not calculate every move; they recognise familiar positions. Patterns are the positions.

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping straight to code before stating the brute force and its cost.
  • Forgetting the extra space (a hash map is O(n) memory).
  • Not checking edge cases: empty input, one element, duplicates, negatives, overflow (use long in Java/Kotlin and long long in C++ when sums can exceed 2^31).

notes.title: Hash map for fast lookups
notes.html:
Idea. A hash map answers "have I seen this before?" in O(1) average time. Many O(n²) "find a pair" problems become O(n) by remembering what you have already seen.

Recognise it when: you need a complement/match for each element (pair sums, duplicates, "first repeated"), or you must count or index things by value.

Worked example: Two Sum (return indices of two numbers adding to target). Brute force checks every pair, O(n²). Instead, for each x, look up target - x in the map of values seen so far.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<int> twoSum(vector<int>& a, int target) {
    unordered_map<int, int> seen;              // value -> index
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        auto it = seen.find(target - a[i]);
        if (it != seen.end()) return {it->second, i};
        seen[a[i]] = i;
    }
    return {};
}
int[] twoSum(int[] a, int target) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();   // value -> index
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        Integer j = seen.get(target - a[i]);
        if (j != null) return new int[]{j, i};
        seen.put(a[i], i);
    }
    return new int[0];
}
fun twoSum(a: IntArray, target: Int): IntArray {
    val seen = HashMap<Int, Int>()                  // value -> index
    for ((i, x) in a.withIndex()) {
        seen[target - x]?.let { return intArrayOf(it, i) }
        seen[x] = i
    }
    return intArrayOf()
}
def two_sum(a, target):
    seen = {}                                       # value -> index
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        if target - x in seen:
            return [seen[target - x], i]
        seen[x] = i
    return []

Complexity. Time O(n), extra space O(n). Check the complement before inserting the current element so an element is never paired with itself.

Language notes for a C++ developer. unordered_map ≈ Java HashMap ≈ Kotlin HashMap/mutableMapOf ≈ Python dict. In Java the get returns a boxed Integer that can be null; in Kotlin seen[key] returns a nullable Int? and ?.let handles the "found" case; Python needs no types.

Everyday analogy. At a party you wonder whether anyone already arrived whose name completes your pair; you keep a guest list instead of re-scanning the whole room.

Common interview traps.

  • Inserting before checking, so [3] with target 6 wrongly returns index 0 twice.
  • Using sort plus two pointers when the indices are required (sorting loses them).
  • Hash-collision worst case is O(n); say "average O(1)".

notes.title: Frequency counting and grouping
notes.html:
Idea. Count how often each value occurs, or group items under a canonical key that is identical for all members of the group.

Recognise it when: anagrams, "most frequent", "first unique character", "group by", comparing multisets.

Worked example: Group Anagrams. Words are anagrams if their sorted letters (or letter counts) match. Use that as the dictionary key.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<vector<string>> groupAnagrams(vector<string>& words) {
    unordered_map<string, vector<string>> groups;
    for (auto& w : words) {
        string key = w;
        sort(key.begin(), key.end());              // canonical form
        groups[key].push_back(w);
    }
    vector<vector<string>> out;
    for (auto& [k, v] : groups) out.push_back(move(v));
    return out;
}
List<List<String>> groupAnagrams(String[] words) {
    Map<String, List<String>> groups = new HashMap<>();
    for (String w : words) {
        char[] c = w.toCharArray();
        Arrays.sort(c);                             // canonical form
        groups.computeIfAbsent(new String(c), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(w);
    }
    return new ArrayList<>(groups.values());
}
fun groupAnagrams(words: List<String>): List<List<String>> =
    words.groupBy { it.toCharArray().sorted().joinToString("") }.values.toList()
from collections import defaultdict

def group_anagrams(words):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for w in words:
        groups["".join(sorted(w))].append(w)       # canonical form
    return list(groups.values())

Complexity. Sorting each word costs O(k log k) for word length k, so O(n · k log k) total. For lowercase letters only, use a 26-count tuple as the key for O(n · k).

Counting tools. C++ unordered_map<char,int> or int cnt[26]; Java int[26]/HashMap; Kotlin groupingBy { it }.eachCount(); Python collections.Counter.

Everyday analogy. Sorting laundry by colour: the colour is the key and each pile is a group.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a mutable list as a dictionary key in Python (use a tuple).
  • Forgetting uppercase letters or Unicode when you assumed a-z and an int[26].

notes.title: Prefix sums
notes.html:
Idea. Precompute prefix[i] = a[0] + ... + a[i-1] so the sum of any range [l, r] is prefix[r+1] - prefix[l] in O(1) after O(n) setup.

Recognise it when: many range-sum queries, "subarray with sum K", "equal 0s and 1s" (map 0 to -1), 2D region sums.

Worked example: Subarray Sum Equals K (count contiguous subarrays summing to k, negatives allowed). A subarray (j, i] sums to k exactly when prefix[i] - prefix[j] = k. Keep a map of how many times each prefix has occurred; for each running sum look up sum - k.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int subarraySum(vector<int>& a, int k) {
    unordered_map<long long, int> cnt{{0, 1}};     // empty prefix
    long long sum = 0; int ans = 0;
    for (int x : a) {
        sum += x;
        auto it = cnt.find(sum - k);
        if (it != cnt.end()) ans += it->second;
        cnt[sum]++;
    }
    return ans;
}
int subarraySum(int[] a, int k) {
    Map<Long, Integer> cnt = new HashMap<>();
    cnt.put(0L, 1);                                 // empty prefix
    long sum = 0; int ans = 0;
    for (int x : a) {
        sum += x;
        ans += cnt.getOrDefault(sum - k, 0);
        cnt.merge(sum, 1, Integer::sum);
    }
    return ans;
}
fun subarraySum(a: IntArray, k: Int): Int {
    val cnt = HashMap<Long, Int>().apply { put(0L, 1) }   // empty prefix
    var sum = 0L
    var ans = 0
    for (x in a) {
        sum += x
        ans += cnt.getOrDefault(sum - k, 0)
        cnt[sum] = cnt.getOrDefault(sum, 0) + 1
    }
    return ans
}
from collections import defaultdict

def subarray_sum(a, k):
    cnt = defaultdict(int)
    cnt[0] = 1                                      # empty prefix
    s = ans = 0
    for x in a:
        s += x
        ans += cnt[s - k]
        cnt[s] += 1
    return ans

Complexity. Time O(n), space O(n). Sliding window does not work here because negative numbers break monotonicity; that is exactly why prefix sums plus a hash map are used.

Industry examples. Cumulative counters in analytics (events per time range), cumulative histograms, and 2D prefix sums for image integral images and region queries.

Everyday analogy. A bank statement's running balance: the money spent between two dates is the difference of two balances.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the base case prefix 0 → count 1, which misses subarrays starting at index 0.
  • Updating the map before looking up sum - k when k = 0 (counts an empty subarray).
  • Overflowing int for large sums.

notes.title: Running state: Kadane's algorithm
notes.html:
Idea. Sometimes a single pass with a small "best so far ending here" state beats prefix arrays. For the maximum subarray sum: at each element either extend the previous subarray or start fresh.

Recognise it when: "maximum/minimum contiguous subarray", single-pass optimisation with a local-versus-global best.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int maxSubArray(vector<int>& a) {
    int cur = a[0], best = a[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        cur = max(a[i], cur + a[i]);               // extend or restart
        best = max(best, cur);
    }
    return best;
}
int maxSubArray(int[] a) {
    int cur = a[0], best = a[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
        cur = Math.max(a[i], cur + a[i]);          // extend or restart
        best = Math.max(best, cur);
    }
    return best;
}
fun maxSubArray(a: IntArray): Int {
    var cur = a[0]
    var best = a[0]
    for (i in 1 until a.size) {
        cur = maxOf(a[i], cur + a[i])              // extend or restart
        best = maxOf(best, cur)
    }
    return best
}
def max_sub_array(a):
    cur = best = a[0]
    for x in a[1:]:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)                      # extend or restart
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

Complexity. O(n) time, O(1) space. It is also the simplest example of dynamic programming: cur is dp[i], the best sum of a subarray ending at i, kept as one variable.

Everyday analogy. A runner's streak: if the current streak turns negative, drop it and start a new one.

Common interview traps.

  • Initialising best = 0 fails on all-negative arrays (the answer is the largest single element).
  • Confusing maximum subarray (contiguous) with maximum subsequence (any elements).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: Read the input size to pick the target complexity, state the brute force, then match a pattern. Hash maps turn "find a pair/duplicate" into O(n) lookups; check the complement before inserting. Frequency counts and canonical keys solve grouping and anagram problems. Prefix sums with a count map solve "subarray sums to K" even with negatives, and need the prefix 0 → 1 base case. Kadane's algorithm keeps one running state to solve maximum-subarray in O(n) time and O(1) space. Watch for overflow, empty input and all-negative arrays.

questions.promptHtml: The input has n = 200,000 elements. Which time complexities are acceptable, and how do you decide?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who cannot estimate cost pick algorithms that time out.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: About 10^8 simple operations run in a second, so for n = 2·10^5 I need O(n) or O(n log n); O(n²) would be 4·10^10 operations and fail. That tells me to think hashing, sorting, heaps, binary search or two pointers instead of nested loops.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Work backwards from constraints: n ≤ 20 suggests exponential backtracking or bitmask; n ≤ 500 allows O(n³); n ≤ 5,000 allows O(n²); n ≥ 10^5 needs O(n log n) or better; 10^9 needs O(log n) or math. Also count memory: an O(n) hash map of 2·10^5 entries is fine, an n×n table is 4·10^10 cells and is not.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Ignoring constants: O(n log n) with a heavy constant can still be slow.
  • Forgetting the cost of sorting or of string concatenation in a loop.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. n = 5,000 and a 2D DP table of ints? → 25M cells, about 100 MB; fine, or roll to two rows.
  2. When is O(n²) acceptable? → n up to a few thousand.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior derives the target from constraints and discusses memory and constants.

questions.promptHtml: Given an array and a target, return the indices of two numbers that add up to the target. Give the optimal solution.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The classic test of moving from O(n²) to O(n) with a hash map.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: One pass with a hash map from value to index. For each element x, check whether target - x is already in the map; if so return those indices, otherwise store x. O(n) time, O(n) space.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Brute force tries every pair, O(n²). The map remembers everything seen so far so each lookup is O(1) average. Check the complement before inserting, so an element is never matched with itself.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<int> twoSum(vector<int>& a, int target) {
    unordered_map<int, int> seen;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        auto it = seen.find(target - a[i]);
        if (it != seen.end()) return {it->second, i};
        seen[a[i]] = i;
    }
    return {};
}
int[] twoSum(int[] a, int target) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        Integer j = seen.get(target - a[i]);
        if (j != null) return new int[]{j, i};
        seen.put(a[i], i);
    }
    return new int[0];
}
fun twoSum(a: IntArray, target: Int): IntArray {
    val seen = HashMap<Int, Int>()
    for ((i, x) in a.withIndex()) {
        seen[target - x]?.let { return intArrayOf(it, i) }
        seen[x] = i
    }
    return intArrayOf()
}
def two_sum(a, target):
    seen = {}
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        if target - x in seen:
            return [seen[target - x], i]
        seen[x] = i
    return []

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Inserting before checking, pairing an element with itself.
  • Sorting first and losing the original indices.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Array is sorted and you may use O(1) space? → Two pointers from both ends.
  2. Return all unique pairs? → Sort plus two pointers, skipping duplicates.
  3. Stream of numbers and many queries? → Keep a counting map and update incrementally.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior states the trade-off between the map (O(n) space) and sort plus two pointers (O(1) space), and notes hash worst case.

questions.promptHtml: Group a list of words into sets of anagrams. What is your key, and what is the complexity?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the "canonical key" idea and awareness of the sort-versus-count trade-off.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use a canonical key that is the same for all anagrams: the sorted characters, or a 26-slot letter-count tuple for lowercase words. Put each word in a map keyed by it. Sorting gives O(n · k log k); the count key gives O(n · k) for word length k.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Anagrams are words with the same multiset of letters, so any representation of that multiset works as a key. In Python the key must be hashable (a tuple, not a list). Choosing the count key avoids the log factor but is only valid for a fixed alphabet.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<vector<string>> groupAnagrams(vector<string>& words) {
    unordered_map<string, vector<string>> g;
    for (auto& w : words) {
        string key = w;
        sort(key.begin(), key.end());
        g[key].push_back(w);
    }
    vector<vector<string>> out;
    for (auto& [k, v] : g) out.push_back(move(v));
    return out;
}
List<List<String>> groupAnagrams(String[] words) {
    Map<String, List<String>> g = new HashMap<>();
    for (String w : words) {
        char[] c = w.toCharArray();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        g.computeIfAbsent(new String(c), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(w);
    }
    return new ArrayList<>(g.values());
}
fun groupAnagrams(words: List<String>): List<List<String>> =
    words.groupBy { it.toCharArray().sorted().joinToString("") }.values.toList()
from collections import defaultdict

def group_anagrams(words):
    g = defaultdict(list)
    for w in words:
        g[tuple(sorted(w))].append(w)
    return list(g.values())

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a list as a Python dict key (unhashable).
  • Assuming only a-z when the input may have capitals or Unicode.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you check if two strings are anagrams? → Compare counts in O(n).
  2. Millions of words? → Stream and group by hash of the count vector; consider memory.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior compares sort key versus count key and discusses the alphabet assumption.

questions.promptHtml: Count the contiguous subarrays whose sum equals K. The array can contain negative numbers.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The standard test of prefix sums plus a hash map; sliding window is a tempting wrong answer.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep a running prefix sum and a map counting how often each prefix has appeared. A subarray ending here sums to K if an earlier prefix equals sum - K, so add that count to the answer, then record the current prefix. Seed the map with 0 → 1. O(n) time and space.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
sum(j+1..i) = prefix[i] - prefix[j]. Sliding window needs all numbers non-negative so the sum moves monotonically; with negatives it does not, so prefix sums plus a map are required.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int subarraySum(vector<int>& a, int k) {
    unordered_map<long long, int> cnt{{0, 1}};
    long long sum = 0; int ans = 0;
    for (int x : a) {
        sum += x;
        auto it = cnt.find(sum - k);
        if (it != cnt.end()) ans += it->second;
        cnt[sum]++;
    }
    return ans;
}
int subarraySum(int[] a, int k) {
    Map<Long, Integer> cnt = new HashMap<>();
    cnt.put(0L, 1);
    long sum = 0; int ans = 0;
    for (int x : a) {
        sum += x;
        ans += cnt.getOrDefault(sum - k, 0);
        cnt.merge(sum, 1, Integer::sum);
    }
    return ans;
}
fun subarraySum(a: IntArray, k: Int): Int {
    val cnt = HashMap<Long, Int>().apply { put(0L, 1) }
    var sum = 0L
    var ans = 0
    for (x in a) {
        sum += x
        ans += cnt.getOrDefault(sum - k, 0)
        cnt[sum] = cnt.getOrDefault(sum, 0) + 1
    }
    return ans
}
from collections import defaultdict

def subarray_sum(a, k):
    cnt = defaultdict(int)
    cnt[0] = 1
    s = ans = 0
    for x in a:
        s += x
        ans += cnt[s - k]
        cnt[s] += 1
    return ans

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Missing the 0 → 1 seed, which misses subarrays starting at index 0.
  • Using int for the running sum when it can overflow.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Longest subarray with sum K? → Store the first index of each prefix instead of a count.
  2. Equal number of 0s and 1s? → Map 0 to -1 and look for sum 0.
  3. 2D matrix region sums? → 2D prefix sums with inclusion-exclusion.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior explains why sliding window fails with negatives and adapts the map for the longest-subarray variant.

questions.promptHtml: Find the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray. Explain why Kadane's algorithm is correct.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A gateway to dynamic programming with O(1) state.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: At each element the best subarray ending here is either the element alone or the previous best extended by it: cur = max(x, cur + x). The answer is the maximum cur seen. O(n) time, O(1) space.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
If the best sum ending at the previous index is negative, extending it only makes things worse, so we restart. It is a DP with dp[i] = max(a[i], dp[i-1] + a[i]) compressed to one variable. Initialising the best to 0 breaks all-negative arrays.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int maxSubArray(vector<int>& a) {
    int cur = a[0], best = a[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        cur = max(a[i], cur + a[i]);
        best = max(best, cur);
    }
    return best;
}
int maxSubArray(int[] a) {
    int cur = a[0], best = a[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
        cur = Math.max(a[i], cur + a[i]);
        best = Math.max(best, cur);
    }
    return best;
}
fun maxSubArray(a: IntArray): Int {
    var cur = a[0]
    var best = a[0]
    for (i in 1 until a.size) {
        cur = maxOf(a[i], cur + a[i])
        best = maxOf(best, cur)
    }
    return best
}
def max_sub_array(a):
    cur = best = a[0]
    for x in a[1:]:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Starting best at 0, failing when all numbers are negative.
  • Confusing subarray (contiguous) with subsequence.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Return the subarray itself? → Track the start index when you restart.
  2. Circular array? → Max of Kadane and total minus the minimum subarray.
  3. Maximum product subarray? → Track both max and min because negatives flip signs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior frames it as DP and handles the circular and product variants.

questions.contextHtml: You are given 10^5 daily sales figures (which can be negative because of refunds) and 10^5 queries of the form "total between day l and day r". Your first solution loops from l to r for every query and the grader times out after 12 seconds.
questions.promptHtml: How do you fix it, and what happens if the sales figures can also be updated?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Micro-optimises the loop or switches language instead of changing the algorithm.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are queries and updates interleaved? Value ranges (overflow)? Are l and r inclusive and 0 or 1 indexed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; this is an algorithm choice.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The brute force is O(n) per query, so 10^5 × 10^5 = 10^10 operations; this is the bottleneck.
  4. How I'd verify: Count operations: 10^10 is about 100 seconds at 10^8 per second.
  5. Root cause: Repeated work; every query re-sums overlapping ranges.
  6. Fix: Build a prefix-sum array once (O(n)) and answer each query as prefix[r+1] - prefix[l] in O(1), for a total of O(n + q). Use 64-bit integers. If there are point updates, use a Fenwick (Binary Indexed) tree or segment tree: O(log n) per update and query.
  7. Prevention: Estimate cost from constraints before coding.
  8. Trade-offs: Prefix sums are static; they use O(n) memory and break under updates, where a Fenwick tree trades O(1) queries for O(log n) updates.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Range updates and range queries? → Segment tree with lazy propagation or two Fenwick trees.
  • 2D region sums? → 2D prefix sums.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A reporting job recomputed range totals per request; precomputing cumulative sums cut a 40-second page to 80 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes the loop.
  • Hire: prefix sums with 64-bit ints.
  • Strong hire: also handles updates with a Fenwick tree and explains the trade-off.
